Burns furnace fuel at %s FE/tick, with a %s FE buffer and at most %s FE/tick output. Each item's fuel credit is its Forge furnace burn time multiplied by the generation rate; coal currently credits %s FE. Burning pauses when a whole tick will not fit. Container fuel requires room for its remainder.

A full oxygen, hydrogen or nitrogen canister represents %s mB of that gas. Fluid-capability exchanges use single canisters; partial finite contents remain stored on the item. Gas types cannot be mixed. Machine slot conversions may require a plain full canister; the gas charge pad accepts only plain oxygen or hydrogen canisters, not nitrogen.

Stores oxygen OR hydrogen, never a mixture. Put a plain filled canister in the input to add %s units and leave an empty canister; put an empty canister in the output slot to fill it from stored gas. Empty-hand use retrieves output; sneaking retrieves input. It does not automatically charge worn suits. Installed pressure tanks are refilled explicitly with matching canisters.

One full oxygen canister supplies %s oxygen units and returns an empty canister; the vent stores %s units. Supply requires a sealed, loaded room and power. The elected provider consumes %s FE/tick and one oxygen unit every %s active ticks before scrubber savings. Open or unavailable rooms are not supplied. Hydrogen is not breathing oxygen.

Put one space-suit armor piece in the armor slot and a compatible module in the component slot, then choose Install. Helmet modules include visors, hover and beacon finder; leg modules include flight speed and bionic legs; feet accept padded landing boots. The chest has a jetpack position and pressure-tank positions. Remove returns the original module, retaining finite tank contents; leave the component slot or a player inventory slot empty. This is an equipment assembly, not a crafting/process recipe.

Supply one chassis, one primary component, up to %s catalog-compatible modules and a blank satellite control chip, with an empty package output. Assemble costs %s FE; each redstone charges %s FE. The server checks the catalog, layout, stats and research. Assembly consumes the components, programs the chip and creates the matching satellite package. Launch the package through a rocket satellite bay; building alone does not deploy it.

Form and power both research multiblocks. Start an observatory survey (%s paid ticks), then claim the ready job at an astrobody data processor (%s paid ticks). Both stages cost %s FE per paid tick. Successful analysis credits %s research once. Surface observation requires visible sky, night and suitable weather; orbital observation uses its station's body context. Jobs belong to their owner and may wait for a server save.

Insert the matching satellite control chip to operate an owned satellite. The terminal starts catalog-defined missions and claims completed data or resource rewards; mission costs, durations and requirements come from the server catalog. A package must be deployed before it becomes an operational satellite. Research credits unlock later catalog operations; this is not a machine process recipe.

Form the orbital laser drill, supply a lens and power, and select a mode. Logical mode draws from the server's body-specific laser table (with its fallback); physical mode needs a linked, loaded laser target and mines its bounded shaft with protection checks. Default cost is %s FE per operation, at a %s-tick interval; server settings can change these. A full output pauses work. The target is an endpoint, not a second recipe machine.

Form the generator in an owned, permitted station orbiting a catalog-defined singularity. Its singularity profile chooses the fuel table and output FE/tick; that table chooses each plain item's burn ticks, including its default for unlisted items. Server energy settings scale the output. A full buffer pauses the burn without spending remaining ticks. This is catalog fuel conversion, not a furnace recipe and not usable at an arbitrary orbit.

An owned, powered area controller applies a permissioned gravity field, not an item conversion. Radius is %s to %s blocks; default radius %s costs %s FE/tick (upkeep is 5 + 2 x radius). Outside stations it affects only the owner and consenting players. Station fields are clipped to the station and capped at normal gravity. Enable the field and check its power, redstone mode and permissions.

Select an active permitted railgun endpoint in the same star system and supply cargo and power. At default energy settings, same-Level/same-body cost is %s + %s x horizontal distance FE, capped at %s FE; other allowed routes cost %s FE and travel for %s ticks. The server ledger retains cargo until the destination records receipt; unavailable destinations wait rather than duplicate cargo. This is transport, not processing.

Bind an anchor and a terminal between a surface and a compatible station orbiting that body, with permitted owners and clear platforms. Default cargo cost is %s FE with %s ticks travel; a player ride costs %s FE after a %s-tick countdown. Server energy settings scale costs. Rides recheck access and the loaded arrival space. A bound pair prevents station warp until unbound. Endpoints provide transport, not process recipes.

Supply power and allow the bounded pump to collect supported source fluid below it. Its fluid capability exposes stored output. Collection checks loaded chunks and protection; it does not load distant chunks or invent fluid from flowing blocks. This is world-fluid collection, not a RecipeManager process.

Generates FE only under suitable sky, light and environment conditions. Connect an energy consumer to take buffered output. There is no fuel or process recipe; crafting obtains the device, while its generation is an environmental service.

Form, power and enable the planetary beacon to publish a navigation marker. A beacon finder installed in a helmet displays eligible markers. The server controls visibility and ownership; an unavailable structure or power supply does not create an active marker. No item-processing recipe is involved.

Place a CO2 scrubber beside its oxygen vent and insert a carbon scrubber cartridge. An eligible bound scrubber saves some vent oxygen debits while spending cartridge durability; it neither creates oxygen nor replaces vent power or room sealing. Recover or remove its cartridge through the device interaction before moving it.

Reports the local atmosphere through redstone. Sneak-use cycles breathable, vacuum, non-breathable atmosphere, high-pressure, hot and cold modes. It observes the server's atmosphere state, not an inferred oxygen concentration; it does not seal or oxygenate a room and has no process recipe.

Use the assembler to scan a bounded block-built rocket, inspect validation failures, then assemble only a valid structure. The server validates components, ownership and inventories before replacing blocks with the rocket. Disassembly restores the accepted structure. This is a world assembly transaction, not an item process recipe.

Load catalog-supported item fuel such as rocket fuel cells into the item fuel loader and link an eligible rocket. Transfer converts accepted items into the rocket's fuel credit under server checks. It does not transfer fluid cargo and cannot supply incompatible propulsion. The catalog defines each item's credit; no furnace burn-time conversion is used here.

Use the linker to bind an eligible rocket, then supply the fluid matching its propulsion role. The server's rocket fluid-fuel catalog defines the conversion and rejects incompatible gas or fuel. This loader fills propulsion tanks; ordinary cargo fluids use rocket fluid loaders instead. Transfer is server-authoritative and is not a process recipe.

Link an owned, compatible rocket and use the appropriate item or fluid loader/unloader for its cargo. Supply or collect resources through the device's capabilities. These devices move cargo under server checks and recovery records; they do not manufacture items, convert propulsion fuel or run processing recipes.

Link an eligible rocket to inspect its server-reported status and use authorized controls. The monitoring station does not assemble a rocket or supply fuel. Its purpose is remote observation/control, with distance, ownership and loaded-state checks, not item processing.

Place a matching owned satellite package in a rocket satellite bay before assembly and flight. Eligible orbital flight deploys it through the server's recorded deployment transaction. The package, bay and rocket must have compatible ownership. A refused deployment retains the package for inspection or retry; the bay does not build satellites.

Bind an owned orbital-energy satellite with its matching control chip and connect an energy consumer. The receiver exposes only energy credited by the satellite service under server eligibility checks. It does not create energy from a chip alone and has no processing recipe.

The warp core bridges a station's stored energy and warp state; the controller is its authorized travel frontend. Select a reachable catalog destination and satisfy station access, fuel/energy and relocation checks. Warp changes the station's logical orbit, not its physical region. A bound space elevator must be unbound first. These are station services, not process machines.

Gravity, altitude and orientation controllers edit the corresponding station properties through server-authorized controls. Use them inside an eligible station with management permission. They do not move arbitrary world blocks, provide area-controller gravity outside a station or process ingredients.

Power and enable an owned projector to maintain its bounded, directional force field. Placement and removal obey loaded-chunk, ownership and protection checks. Field blocks belong to that projector and are not obtainable crafting outputs; disabling or removing the projector removes its valid claims. There is no item process recipe.
